screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Nutrition & Hydration queue positions 17-57. Drafted by Claude Haiku 5.5 and claim-audited against source text by Claude Opus 5.5 (docs/haiku-calibration/).

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Undeclared doping substances are highly prevalent in commercial sports nutrition supplements.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional laboratory survey of 66 high-risk sports nutrition supplements (claiming hormone modulation, muscle gain, fat loss or energy) bought from 17 Dutch web shops in December 2014 and tested by an accredited anti-doping laboratory. Undeclared doping substances were found in 25 products (38%), including high levels of synthetic stimulants in three. The authors estimate that three products could impose general health risks at the recommended dose, and that several high-level findings could produce a positive doping test.
records.limitations: Products were bought in 2014, so the prevalence reflects that market and a preselected high-risk subset rather than today's products. Low-level findings were qualitative, and exposure estimates assume maximum recommended doses and reference medicine values. The trend comparison with earlier surveys rests on data not shown.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 38% figure as the chance that any supplement is contaminated, when the sample was a purposive set of high-risk products bought in 2014 and is not a random sample of the market.

changes: paper.findings: low-level findings described as 'mainly the steroids boldione and 17alpha-AED, plus higenamine', omitting the stimulant DMAA, which was as frequent as 17alpha-AED -> counts added ('boldione was detected the most (11 findings) followed by ... 17α-AED and the stimulant 4-methylhexan-2-amine (both 6 findings). The beta-2 agonist higenamine was detected 4 times')
verification.residualConcerns: The 38% depends on reporting thresholds the authors applied for steroids and ephedrine; without them 50% of products would have been positive.

records.sourceFile: Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Two free-living cohorts (Study 1, 58 participants for 3 days; Study 2, 35 participants for 7 days) of healthy adults aged 18 to 35 (93 total, 47 female) provided reference change values for body mass, urine color and thirst, then Study 2 underwent 2 hours of passive heating followed by random assignment to control, sweat-loss or fluid-restriction conditions. Body mass change, urine color and thirst each separated the groups for predicted dehydration probability, and ridge regression gave body mass 58% and thirst 26% of relative importance in the weighted WUT model.
records.limitations: Participants were healthy, non-athlete young adults who exercised no more than 10 hours a week, and the authors say results may not transfer to athletes, older adults or people with illness. The model was fitted and tested on the same data without a holdout set, and the authors caution that the importance weights may be overfitted.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could take the 58% and 26% weightings or the 90% dehydration probabilities as validated athlete hydration thresholds, when they come from healthy non-athlete young adults (free-living data plus a 35-person heat and 24 h fluid-manipulation protocol), with no athlete data.

changes: paper.findings: urine color result attributed p = 0.044 to the restriction vs control comparison -> 0.044 is the overall ANOVA and the restriction vs control post-hoc was p = 0.047 ('Restriction (Mean +/- SD, 0.832 +/- 0.143, p = 0.047)')

synthesisCaution: said the 90% probabilities came from the 2-hour heat protocol -> they come from reference change values in the free-living data ('Using the free-living data (Study 1 and Study 2), the reference change values (RCV) were calculated')
paper.limitations: added the small manipulation sample and the internal conflict between CI and p value ('0.34 [95% CI, -0.11, 0.57]' with 'p = 0.003')

records.sourceFile: Vitamin C supplementation and athletic performance - A review.pdf
records.degradedReason: The article's own DOI is not printed in the text; only the journal name and URL appear.

changes: paper.citation: added printed pages 255-259 ('Volume 22 Number 7 July 2023'; '1537-890X/2207/255-259')

paper.findings: added that all three positive trials used co-supplementation and that 'Vitamin C alone did not appear to have a positive effect on markers of muscle damage with long-term supplementation'; specified blunted adaptations came from vitamin C plus vitamin E trials; 'Most studies used vitamin C with at least one other supplement' -> 'Only two studies used vitamin C alone' ('only two of the studies supplemented with vitamin C alone')
verification.residualConcerns: Own DOI not printed; operator should verify externally before upgrading the decision.

records.sourceFile: Vitamin D and the Athlete- Current                        Perspectives and New Challenges.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of vitamin D in athletes, covering bone health, extra-skeletal roles in muscle, immunity and cardiac structure, the safety of high-dose supplementation and the role of ethnicity and bioavailable vitamin D. No systematic search is described. The authors report that serum 25(OH)D has consistently failed to show a relationship with bone health in athletes, describe possible effects on recovery and infection risk, and raise concern about very high doses.
records.limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, so the choice of evidence cannot be checked, and it includes the authors' own laboratory data. The article is part of a supplement from an expert panel meeting, and one author received honoraria from GSSI, a division of PepsiCo.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat free (bioavailable) vitamin D testing as an established standard, but the authors note that no gold-standard assay or validated thresholds exist yet and that new thresholds still need to be set.

changes: evidenceSummary: 'a weak link between serum 25(OH)D and bone health' -> no consistent relationship ('data have consistently failed to demonstrate any relationship between serum 25[OH]D and bone health'); added cardiac structure to the coverage list

synthesisCaution: 'the review only calls for re-examining the data, not for a validated clinical test' -> the review does recommend free vitamin D assays when testing is warranted, but no gold standard exists ('If testing is warranted, practitioners should use the appropriate assays to determine bioavailable (free) vitamin D'; 'No comparison of techniques and establishment of a gold standard have yet been reported')

paper.athleteDev: 'possible toxicity' -> the concern is a raised catabolite at 70,000 IU/week ('the highest dose (70,000 IU/week) also raised the product of vitamin D catabolism, 24,25[OH]D'); 'largely mechanistic' -> mechanistic, observational or small trial data
paper.practicalImplications: added the authors' advice against 'blanket approaches to supplementation, mega doses of vitamin D, bolus doses' and their preference for bioavailable assays
paper.findings: added the authors' observation of smaller cardiac dimensions in severely deficient athletes
verification.residualConcerns: Includes cardiac and supplement-dosing content; cardiac findings come from the authors' own cross-sectional study.
